overview.title: Chapter 10 opener: Interpreting what ConvNets learn
overview.main_topic: Why interpretability matters for computer vision models, and why ConvNets, unlike many deep learning models, are not 'black boxes'
overview.central_idea: Interpretability, understanding why a classifier made a decision, is a fundamental problem in computer vision, particularly when deep learning complements human expertise as in medical imaging. ConvNets learn representations of visual concepts, which makes them highly amenable to visualization; the chapter teaches several such techniques.
overview.importance: It shifts the book from building better ConvNets (chapters 8–9) to understanding and debugging them, a skill needed to trust, diagnose and improve vision models.

Explain what interpretability means for an image classifier
Explain why the 'black box' criticism applies less to ConvNets

summary:
This is the opening page of **chapter 10, "Interpreting what ConvNets learn"** (PDF pp.308–331). The box **This chapter covers** lists three topics:

- interpreting how ConvNets **decompose an input image** (intermediate activations, section 10.1, p.309),
- **visualizing the filters** learned by ConvNets (section 10.2, p.315),
- visualizing the **areas of an image responsible for a classification decision** (class activation heatmaps, section 10.3, p.323).

The chapter outline also includes section 10.4, visualizing the latent space of a ConvNet (p.330).

The first paragraph frames the problem of **interpretability**: *why* did your classifier think an image contained a fridge when all you can see is a truck? This matters most when deep learning **complements human expertise**, as in **medical imaging**, where a prediction alone is not enough and practitioners need to see what drove it. The chapter introduces a range of techniques for visualizing what ConvNets learn and understanding their decisions.

The second paragraph addresses the common claim that deep learning models are **"black boxes"** whose representations are hard to extract and present in human-readable form. The authors grant that this is partly true for some models, but **definitely not for ConvNets**: their representations are highly amenable to visualization, largely because they are **representations of visual concepts**. The sentence beginning "Since 2013, a…" continues on p.309, which lists the techniques the chapter will cover.

Use this page as a map for the chapter. Sections 10.2 and 10.3 come in TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX versions (pp.318–319, 326–327).

paragraphs.excerpt: A fundamental problem when building a computer vision application is that of interpretability:
paragraphs.what_it_says: Interpretability is a fundamental problem in computer vision: why did the classifier think an image contained a fridge when you can see a truck? It matters especially where deep learning complements human expertise, such as medical imaging. The chapter introduces techniques for visualizing what ConvNets learn and understanding their decisions.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Accuracy numbers do not tell you *why* a model is right or wrong. Interpretation tools let you check whether the model looks at the right evidence, which helps you debug errors and decide whether to trust it.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: In high-stakes domains, a human expert has to judge whether a model's reasoning makes sense before acting on it.

terminology.meaning: The ability to explain or understand why a model produced a particular output.

connections: p.309: lists the specific visualization techniques

paragraphs.excerpt: It’s often said that deep learning models are “black boxes”: they learn representations
paragraphs.what_it_says: Deep learning models are often called black boxes because their representations are hard to extract and present in human-readable form. This is partly true for some models but definitely not for ConvNets, whose representations are highly amenable to visualization because they are representations of visual concepts. The sentence continues on p.309.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A ConvNet's intermediate outputs are themselves image-like grids, so you can plot them directly and see what they respond to (edges, textures, object parts), unlike the abstract vectors of many other models.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It justifies the whole chapter: ConvNets are among the most inspectable deep learning models.

terminology.meaning: A system whose internal workings cannot be inspected or understood, only its inputs and outputs.

connections: p.291: ConvNets work by learning a hierarchy of modular patterns and concepts to represent the visual world

concepts.name: Interpretability
concepts.definition: Understanding why a model makes the decisions it makes.
concepts.intuition: Asking the model to show what it looked at, not just its answer.
concepts.technical: For ConvNets: visualizing intermediate activations, filters, class activation heatmaps and latent spaces (chapter 10).
concepts.significance: Essential when models complement human expertise, e.g. medical imaging.
concepts.example: A classifier labels a truck as a fridge; a heatmap could show which image regions drove that decision.
concepts.misconception: That all deep learning models are uninterpretable black boxes. ConvNets are highly amenable to visualization.

questions.question: What are the three topics listed in the 'This chapter covers' box?
questions.answer: Interpreting how ConvNets decompose an input image; visualizing the filters learned by ConvNets; visualizing areas in an image responsible for a certain classification decision.

questions.question: Why, according to the authors, are ConvNets highly amenable to visualization?
options: Because they have fewer parameters than other models
Because their representations are representations of visual concepts
Because they use only linear layers
Because they are trained with data augmentation
questions.answer: Because their representations are representations of visual concepts
questions.explanation: The text gives exactly this reason. Parameter count, linearity (ConvNets are non-linear) and augmentation are not the reason given.

questions.question: Why is interpretability especially relevant in medical imaging?
questions.answer: Because the model complements human experts, who need to understand and verify why it made a decision before relying on it.
questions.explanation: The page names use cases where deep learning complements human expertise, giving medical imaging as the example.

questions.question: Before reading on, can you guess what an 'intermediate activation' of a ConvNet would look like when plotted?
questions.answer: A set of 2D images, one per channel of a layer's output feature map, each highlighting where a learned pattern appears in the input.
questions.explanation: Section 10.1 (p.309) confirms that each channel is plotted independently as a 2D image.

questions.question: What claim about deep learning models do the authors partially reject on this page?
questions.answer: That they are 'black boxes' whose learned representations cannot be extracted and presented in human-readable form.
questions.explanation: They accept it for certain models but say it is definitely not true for ConvNets.
